literal: Official Posts Treatise III ○ Southern Face
idiomatic: Official Posts Treatise III — Southern Face

literal: From Emperor Taizong of Tang the Khitan state had commandery governors and prefects appointed; Empress Wu added princely enfeoffments; Emperor Xuanzong set up frontier commissioners—only then did Tang titles and ranks appear.
idiomatic: Under Tang, the Khitan first received commandery governors and prefects, then princely titles from Empress Wu, then frontier commissioners from Xuanzong—Tang office and rank had arrived.

literal: Afterward they grew accustomed to hearing that the Hebei frontier commands received Tang office names, and so Grand Preceptor, Grand Guardian, Grand Tutor, and Grand Commandant were applied within the tribes.
idiomatic: They then heard how Hebei military governors took Tang titles, and Grand Preceptor, Grand Guardian, Grand Tutor, and Grand Commandant spread through the tribes.

literal: Taizu followed this practice.
idiomatic: Taizu adopted the same practice.

literal: In Datong year 1, Shizong first established the Northern Court Privy Commissioner.
idiomatic: Shizong created the Northern Court Privy Commissioner in Datong year 1.

literal: The next year Shizong appointed Gao Xun Southern Court privy commissioner; the establishment of the privy commission thus began when Taizong entered Bian.
idiomatic: The next year Gao Xun became Southern privy commissioner—the privy posts date from Taizong's entry into Bian.

literal: In Tianlu year 4 the Directorate of Governance was founded.
idiomatic: Tianlu year 4 saw the Directorate of Governance established.

literal: Only then could Southern Face bureaucracy be set down in writing.
idiomatic: Southern Face offices could then be recorded in full.

literal: At first the Han Privy Council also held the Department of State Affairs: Personnel, War, and Justice had receivers; Revenue and Works had clerks; the Secretariat also held Rites, and there was a separate Revenue Commissioner Office.
idiomatic: Initially the Han Privy Council doubled as the Department of State Affairs—Personnel, War, and Justice had receivers, Revenue and Works had clerks, the Secretariat held Rites, and a separate Revenue Commissioner Office existed.

literal: With Yingzhou territory added to half of You and Ji, that was just sufficient.
idiomatic: Adding Yingzhou to half of You and Ji made the arrangement adequate.

literal: In the mid-reign titles multiplied: Yelu Yangliu as Grand Preceptor showed that the Three Preceptors existed.
idiomatic: Mid-dynasty titles proliferated—Yelu Yangliu as Grand Preceptor revealed the Three Preceptors.

literal: Huguzhi as Grand Commandant showed that the Three Dukes existed.
idiomatic: Huguzhi as Grand Commandant showed the Three Dukes were in place.

literal: Yuwangde as Regular Attendant and Liu Jing as Minister of Rites showed that the Gate and Ministries existed.
idiomatic: Yuwangde as Regular Attendant and Liu Jing as Minister of Rites showed Gate and Ministry institutions.

literal: Revenue, Works, and Granary section vice-directors sent on missions showed the complement of bureau directors and constellation officers.
idiomatic: Vice-directors of Revenue, Works, and Granary sections on mission showed how many bureau and constellation posts were filled.

literal: Shi Fang as supervising compiler showed that there was a National History Academy.
idiomatic: Shi Fang supervising compilation showed a National History Academy.

literal: Cheng Xu as Secretariat Gentleman showed that there were court diaries.
idiomatic: Cheng Xu as Secretariat Gentleman showed court diary keepers.

literal: Xing Baopu as receiver and Wang Yanfu as academician showed that there was Hanlin internal drafting.
idiomatic: Xing Baopu as receiver and Wang Yanfu as academician showed Hanlin internal drafting.

literal: Zhang Gan as Secretariat policy drafter showed that there was Secretariat external drafting.
idiomatic: Zhang Gan as policy drafter showed Secretariat external drafting.

literal: Grand Court of Review and Grand Granary had directors; Directorate of Education and Palace Workshops had supervisors—the Nine Directors and array of supervisors appeared.
idiomatic: Review and Granary had directors; Education and Palace Workshops had supervisors—the Nine Directors and supervisory offices appeared.

literal: Golden Crow and Thousand-Ox had generals—the sixteen guards appeared.
idiomatic: Golden Crow and Thousand-Ox had generals, revealing the sixteen guards.

literal: Above the Heir Apparent were preceptors and guardians; below were commandery rates—Eastern Palace supporting offices too.
idiomatic: The Heir Apparent had preceptors and guardians above and commandery rates below—full Eastern Palace staff.

literal: Military commissioners, observation commissioners, defense commissioners, training commissioners, and prefects all stood in the provinces, as under Tang institutions.
idiomatic: Military, observation, defense, and training commissioners and prefects sat in the provinces as in Tang.

literal: Liao already had Northern Face palace offices; once it held the sixteen prefectures of Yan and Dai it adopted Tang institutions and re-established Southern Face Secretariat, Six Ministries, courts, academies, directorates, guards, and Eastern Palace offices.
idiomatic: With Northern Face offices in place, seizing Yan and Dai's sixteen prefectures brought Tang institutions back—Southern Secretariat, Six Ministries, courts, academies, directorates, guards, and Eastern Palace posts.

literal: Truly it wished to model the splendor of imperial institutions—and also to win over subjects of China.
